    Instructor Notes

    The session in one sentence

    One hour, run as a single exercise: the presenter gives a prompt, pairs carry it out on the beach water quality workbook, and the presenter draws the principle from what they find. Learners have the prompts on the Session prompts page; this page holds the run sheet, the debrief points and the answer keys.

    Place in the workshop

    This is the last session of the Using AI in Postgraduate Studies workshop. It follows Prof Randhir Rawatlal’s session, Working with generative AI on a postgraduate project, and deliberately repeats his practices on a dataset, so learners meet each one a second time in use. Name the link aloud each time it comes up. The RR column below gives the minute in his session plan.

    Here RR His point How it returns here
    Step 1 0-5 Raw data never edited Copy the tab before touching it
    Step 3 45-50 Flag faulty data Flag columns for <10, TNTC; a reason column for blanks
    Check 1 40-45 Test on cases with known answers The −26.0 fails a sanity check; 149.7 is the known answer for Topic 2
    Step 5 5-10 Standing instructions read every session The data dictionary is the data’s standing instructions
    Step 7 30-34 Repeated, checkable work goes to a tool Ask for the code, not just the number
    Step 8 0-5, 10-13 Repository; log line; which model may read which file raw/processed folders; a log line for Step 7; four POPIA cases

    If the order of sessions changes, change “as Prof Rawatlal showed” to “as Prof Rawatlal will show” and keep the links.

    Before the session

    • Data. Check that the links on the Setup page download. Put the zip on the LAN share, or on the desktop of each LAN machine, as a fallback.
    • LAN. Confirm that the LAN machines have Excel or LibreOffice, a browser, and access to chatgpt.com, claude.ai and gemini.google.com.
    • Chat models. The demonstrators test Steps 6 and 7 on a free account with each of ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini the day before, note any upload limits, and keep screenshots of the answers for the projector.
    • Projector. The presenter’s machine has the workbook, the tidy CSV and a logged-in chat model open in separate windows, at large font size.
    • Print. A few copies of both data tabs of the messy workbook, for pairs without a device, and the prompt sheet.
    • Sticky notes. Two colours: one for “stuck”, one for the closing commitment.

    Demonstrators

    Two demonstrators circulate, one on each side of the room (or one in the LAN if it is used). Brief them on:

    • Excel on Windows and macOS, LibreOffice and Google Sheets menus for Move or Copy, Sort, Filter, Save As CSV UTF-8 and Data Validation.
    • Sorting a whole block, never one column (“Expand the selection”).
    • Attaching a file in each chat model, and pasting CSV text when uploads fail.
    • Not giving answers during Steps 2 and 5; ask “what would a program see here?” instead.

    Run sheet

    Topic 1 · The table a machine can read

    0-5 · Step 1, find the mean. Prompt: “Copy a tab, then use AVERAGE for North Beach 2024.” Expected: −26.0. Ask: “Would you put this in a thesis? A count of bacteria cannot be negative.” Point out that they copied the tab first: raw data are never edited (RR 0-5). Do not explain the −26 yet.

    5-10 · Step 2, what stops a computer? Prompt: “List everything that would stop a program, or a model, reading this sheet.” Take four or five answers. From them, state the three rules: each variable in a column, each observation in a row, one value in each cell. Use Sipho’s two side-by-side blocks as the example (episode 1).

    10-15 · Step 3, sort and filter. Prompt: “Sort the counts largest to smallest; filter the site column.” Expected: text (55 cfu, <10) sorts above the numbers, -999 sits at the bottom of them, blanks at the very end. Lerato’s filter shows thirteen names for four beaches. Debrief: a blank plus a missing_reason column, flag columns for censored values (RR 45-50), a fixed list enforced by a drop-down (episode 4). Demonstrate the drop-down in one minute if time allows.

    15-20 · Step 4, what day is A9? Prompt: “What date is A9? Save as CSV UTF-8, open in a text editor, then in Excel.” Expected: A9 04/02/2024 reads as 4 February in South Africa; the weekly schedule shows it is 2 April. 12 Mar gains the current year on reopening. Debrief: ISO 8601, CSV UTF-8 as the master copy (episodes 3 and 5).

    20-30 · Check 1. Pairs tick their Step 2 list against Key 1 (on the projector), then compute the mean from the tidy CSV. Explain the −26 now: (308 + 54 − 999 + 114 + 252 + 115) / 6 = −26.0. AVERAGE counted -999 as a number and silently skipped 55 cfu and <10 because they are text. The measured counts give 149.7, n = 6. Point out that 149.7 is now a known answer: anything that reports otherwise in Topic 2 is wrong (RR 40-45).

    Topic 2 · Giving the model its context

    30-35 · Step 5, write the dictionary. Prompt: “Without looking, define sample_id, collector, above_count_range, water_temp_c and notes.” Then compare with the dictionary file. Typical gaps: the upper count limit (2000 cfu/100 mL), the temperature unit, that sample_id is never reused. Link: the dictionary is to the data what Prof Rawatlal’s initialisation file is to a project, the standing instructions the model reads every time (RR 5-10).

    35-40 · Step 6, ask the model, messy. Prompt: “Ask a free chat model for the North Beach 2024 mean from the messy workbook.” Pairs write down the answer and whether the model mentioned -999, <10 or 55 cfu. Answers vary by model and by run; collect three or four aloud. That variation is the point.

    40-45 · Step 7, ask the model, tidy. Prompt: “Attach the tidy CSV and dictionary, use the prompt on the sheet, and ask for the code.” Pairs compare with the known answer and read which rows the code kept. Link: asking for the code turns a conversation into a tool you can check and re-run (RR 30-34).

    45-50 · Step 8, your own data. Prompt: “Sketch your project folder, log Step 7 in one line, and decide the four cases.” Keep the debrief short; Prof Rawatlal has covered the repository and data classes (RR 0-5, 10-13). Stress only what is new: raw is read-only and files flow one way to processed and outputs (episode 7).

    50-60 · Check 2. Key 2 on the projector. Close by asking each learner to write on a sticky note one change they will make to their own data this week.

    Key 1 · Problems planted in the messy workbook

    Nineteen problems. Pairs typically find eight to twelve. Each is described in episode 2.

    # Problem Where
    1 Two tables side by side on one tab 2024 Sipho, A-D and F-I
    2 Two tabs for one kind of data, with different column names, order and units 2024 Sipho, 2025_Lerato (final) v2
    3 Merged cells Sipho A1:I1, A3:D3, F3:I3
    4 Title and legend inside the data Sipho A1, A15
    5 Blank: zero, missing or forgotten? Sipho G9
    6 -999 as a missing-value code, counted by AVERAGE Sipho B7; Summary B3 gives −26.0
    7 Censored values typed as text <10: Sipho B10, G7; Lerato C6, C30. TNTC: Sipho G6
    8 Units typed into number cells 55 cfu Sipho B8; Lerato C5, C13, C21, C28, C35. 23.0C throughout Lerato column D
    9 Numbers stored as text Sipho temperatures C6, C7, C9, C10, C12 and H6, H7, H9, H10, H12
    10 Five date formats, one with no year Sipho A5-A9; Lerato column B
    11 Ambiguous day and month Sipho A9 04/02/2024 (2 April); Lerato B5, B11, B16, B22, B27, B32 are month-first. B11 03/04/2025 is 4 March, not 3 April
    12 Thirteen spellings of four beaches, including trailing spaces Lerato column A (A5, A9 end in a space)
    13 Colour carries meaning Red = above a guideline (Sipho, Lerato); yellow = “exclude” (Lerato rows 5-6); Summary B5 asks for a count of red cells
    14 Information in a cell comment Sipho B6: “Retest? Lab said contamination possible”
    15 More than one value in a cell Lerato column E (tide / sea state); F8 (two counts, two categories)
    16 A calculation inside the data Lerato row 10, Mean North Beach, which averages only six of eight values (101.7)
    17 Header repeated part-way down Lerato row 19
    18 Fahrenheit among Celsius Lerato D14, 74.1 °F = 23.4 °C
    19 Problem column names and special characters Entero (cfu/100mL), Temp °C, Site / tide; Lerato F12 has an em-dash and curly quotes from WhatsApp; tab name 2025_Lerato (final) v2

    A trap worth showing. Summary B4 gives the Addington 2024 mean as 102.8, which matches the tidy answer. It is right by luck: there is no -999 in that column, and AVERAGE dropped TNTC, <10 and the blank, which the tidy calculation also excludes. A correct number from a broken method is still a broken method.

    Key 2 · Model runs and the four cases

    Step 6 (messy). No single right answer. Look for whether the model noticed the two-table layout, treated -999 as missing, and said what it did with <10 and 55 cfu. Some models report −26.0; some report a number near 149.7 without saying which cells they dropped; a few ask a clarifying question. Only the last behaviour is acceptable without checking.

    Step 7 (tidy). The full answer, for checking any model’s output:

    Site Year Mean (cfu/100 mL) n Below detection Above range Missing (reason)
    North Beach 2024 149.7 6 1 0 1 (bottle_broken)
    Addington 2024 102.8 5 1 1 1 (not_sampled_rough_sea)
    North Beach 2025 112.4 7 1 0 0
    Addington 2025 215.6 8 0 0 0
    uShaka 2025 48.2 8 0 0 0
    Umhlanga Main 2025 144.3 7 1 0 0

    Step 8 (four cases).

    1. Yes. The beach data are synthetic and CC-BY.
    2. Only with conditions. Check the funder agreement; use an institution-approved tool.
    3. No, not as it stands. Student numbers and marks are personal information under POPIA. Remove them first, or use an approved tool.
    4. No, unless participants consented and the ethics approval allows it. Anonymise first.

    A good log line for Step 7:

    2026-11-10  JP  Mean count per site and year from tidy CSV, with dictionary;
                Claude (free), prompt in docs/prompts/2026-11-10_means.txt;
                checked North Beach 2024 against known answer 149.7, n = 6.

    If there are no devices

    • Steps 1-4: pairs mark problems on the printout; the presenter performs each prompt on the projector.
    • Steps 6-7: a demonstrator runs both queries on the projector, or shows the screenshots taken the day before.
    • Steps 5 and 8 need only paper.

    Common problems

    • Excel looks different on every machine. Do not demonstrate menus at length; the demonstrators handle them pair by pair.
    • Opening files from inside the zip. Excel opens them read-only. Unzip first.
    • Uploads refused on a free account. Paste the CSV text into the chat instead; open the CSV in a text editor, select all, copy.
    • A quiet room at Step 2. Start the list yourself with one problem, or ask a demonstrator for theirs.
